examples.scenario: Misconfigured AWS S3 bucket allowing public read-write access leading to unauthorized data exposure and data tampering.

S3_access_logs_sample: 79a5d3e9e3e2f7a2 123456789012 [20/May/2024:13:42:55 +0000] 203.0.113.45 arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/anonymous ANONYMOUS EXAMPLE-SENSITIVE-BUCKET REST.PUT.OBJECT malicious-shell.php "PUT /example-sensitive-bucket/malicious-shell.php HTTP/1.1" 200 - - 123 15 10 - "curl/7.79.1" -

79a5d3e9e3e2f7a3 123456789012 [20/May/2024:13:45:21 +0000] 198.51.100.22 arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/anonymous ANONYMOUS EXAMPLE-SENSITIVE-BUCKET REST.GET.OBJECT confidential/customer_data.csv "GET /example-sensitive-bucket/confidential/customer_data.csv HTTP/1.1" 200 - - 2048 38 20 - "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www.google.com/bot.html)" -

indicators: S3 bucket policy granting s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject to Principal '*' (everyone).
CloudTrail logs showing PutObject and GetObject events from anonymous (unauthenticated) users.
S3 access logs showing HTTP PUT requests from external IPs uploading suspicious files like shell.php.
Presence of web shell code in uploaded PHP file (shell.php).
Bucket ACLs granting FULL_CONTROL permissions to AllUsers group.
Unusual user agents such as curl or automated bots accessing sensitive objects.
examples.detection_method: Automated scanning of bucket policies and ACLs for public read-write permissions using CSPM tools (e.g., AWS Config rules, ScoutSuite), correlation of CloudTrail event logs for anonymous PutObject or DeleteObject events, monitoring S3 access logs for HTTP methods and user-agent anomalies, and alerting on presence of executable files uploaded to buckets not intended for public content.
